'''Regine Kahmann''' (born 20 October 1948 in [[Staßfurt]], Saxony-Anhalt) is a German microbiologist and was Director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology]] in [[Marburg]] from 2000 to 2019.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Prof. Regine Kahmann – AcademiaNet|url=https://www.academia-net.org/profil/prof-regine-kahmann/1133817|access-date=23 July 2020|website=www.academia-net.org}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=CV Regine Kahmann|url=https://www.mpi-marburg.mpg.de/651992/Regine-Kahmann|access-date=23 July 2020|website=www.mpi-marburg.mpg.de|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=14 December 2001|title=Neu im Universitätsrat: Prof. Regine Kahmann|url=http://www.uni-heidelberg.de/presse/news/2111kahmann.html|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011214083544/http://www.uni-heidelberg.de/presse/news/2111kahmann.html|archive-date=14 December 2001|access-date=23 July 2020}}</ref> She was made a [[Fellow of the Royal Society|Foreign Member of the Royal Society]] (ForMRS) in 2020.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Outstanding scientists elected as Fellows and Foreign Members of the Royal Society {{!}} Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2020/04/outstanding-scientists-elected-as-fellows-and-foreign-members-of-the-royal-society/|access-date=23 July 2020|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb}}</ref>

Kahmann's early work focused on microbiology and phages. She later switched to studying [[Corn smut|corn smut (''Ustilago maydis'')]], and the causes of disease in maize. Corn smut is now considered a [[model organism]] for the study of biotrophic fungi.<ref name="Kahmann"/>

==Early life== 
Regine Kahmann was born in Staßfurt, Saxony-Anhalt<ref name="NAS">{{cite web |title=Regine Kahmann |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/regine-kahmann-5snaml/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref> in 1948 to Werner and Elfriede Kahmann. Her parents were farmers in Langenweddingen, near [[Magdeburg]] in [[East Germany]]. Due to land reform and political repression, her family left the German Democratic Republic in 1952, settling in Rassau, near [[Uelzen]] in Lower Saxony.<ref name="Kahmann"/>

== Career ==
After graduating from the Lessing School in Uelzen in 1967, Kahmann studied biology at the [[University of Göttingen]] with a focus on microbiology until 1972.<ref name=":2" /> Following her doctorate from 1972 to 1974 at the [[Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics]] and the [[Free University of Berlin]] with the theme ''The structure of SPP1 DNA after transfection of B. subtilis''.<ref name=":0" /> As a postdoctoral fellow, she went to [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]] in the US, where she became in 1976 Junior Group Leader. From 1980 to 1982, she worked as a research assistant at the [[Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry|Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry]] in [[Martinsried]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1982, she started an independent research group at the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics in Berlin followed by appointments at the Institute of Gene-Biological Research in Berlin (1987), and professor of genetics at the Institute for Genetics and Microbiology at [[LMU Munich]] (1992). In January 2000, Kahmann became a scientific member of the [[Max Planck Society]] and director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology]] in Marburg, and in April 2001 also a professor of genetics at [[Marburg University]]. In 2019, she became the acting head of the Department of Organismic Interactions at the Max Planck Institute in Marburg.<ref name=":1" />

== Research ==
Kahmann works in the field of the molecular [[Plant pathology|phytopathology]] – the molecular basis of plant diseases. She examines, among other things, how microbes and viruses infect cells and which genes influence these attacks.<ref name=":0" /> "In her work on [[Muvirus|phage mu]] – a virus that affects a whole range of bacterial species – Regine Kahmann was able to show, among other things, that the decision as to which host can be infected is regulated by inversion of a certain section of DNA. The inversion is done by [[site-specific recombination]]. Regine Kahmann was able to show that this process is stimulated by the bacterial host's FIS protein in addition to the actual recombinase, the elucidation of the stimulation mechanism is internationally considered a scientific masterpiece."<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Leopoldina ehrt die Molekularbiologin Regine Kahmann mit der Mendel-Medaille (13.09.2011)|url=https://www.leopoldina.org/de/presse/pressemitteilungen/pressemitteilung/press/989/|access-date=23 July 2020|website=www.leopoldina.org|language=de}}</ref>

A major research focus in her lab is the investigation of the infection mechanism of a parasitic fungus, [[Corn smut|corn smut (''Ustilago maydis'')]], which causes tumors on maize plants.<ref name="Kahmann">{{cite journal |last1=Kahmann |first1=Regine |title=My Personal Journey from the Fascination for Phages to a Tumor-Inducing Fungal Pathogen of Corn |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |date=8 September 2022 |volume=76 |issue=1 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1146/annurev-micro-121721-111032 |pmid=35395169 |s2cid=248050525 |language=en |issn=0066-4227}}</ref>
